meta.title: Who really said "Research Is to See What Everybody Else Has Seen and Think What Nobody Has Thought"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Schopenhauer wrote the thought in German in 1851 — but not this sentence. The English form first appears, unsigned, in Szent-Györgyi's Bioenergetics (1957).
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Research Is to See What Everybody Else Has Seen and Think What Nobody Has Thought'?
meta.ogDescription: The idea is Schopenhauer's, from Parerga und Paralipomena § 76 (1851). The famous wording is a 1950s compression nobody signed — and Szent-Györgyi quoted it.

answer.label: Not Schopenhauer's words — his thought, compressed
answer.sourceLine: The idea is genuinely Schopenhauer’s: he set it down in German in 1851, in § 76 of the second volume of Parerga und Paralipomena. The sentence is not. Schopenhauer never used the word “research,” and Quote Investigator ↗ traces the snappy English form to a 1957 epigraph in Albert Szent-Györgyi’s Bioenergetics — where Szent-Györgyi himself printed it inside quotation marks, signalling he was quoting somebody else.

source.heading: Where it actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Parerga und Paralipomena: Kleine Philosophische Schriften
Volume 2, § 76, page 93 — A. W. Hayn, Berlin, 1851
German. The passage contains no word for “research.”
None by Schopenhauer’s hand. The popular English sentence is an anonymous twentieth-century compression, not a translation of § 76.

source.excerpt: Daher ist die Aufgabe nicht sowohl zu sehen was noch keiner gesehen hat, als bei Dem was Jeder sieht, zu denken was noch Keiner gedacht hat. Darum auch gehört so sehr viel mehr dazu, ein Philosoph als ein Physiker zu seyn.
trail: 1851 — the real origin. Schopenhauer publishes Parerga und Paralipomena in Berlin. Quote Investigator ↗ locates the sentence at volume 2, § 76, page 93 of the A. W. Hayn edition — in German, with no mention of research and a closing jab at physicists.

1934 and 1952 — faithful translations that nobody repeats. The same chronology records English renderings by Jan Willem Moll in Phytography as a Fine Art (1934) and Ludwig von Bertalanffy in Problems of Life (1952). Both credit Schopenhauer by name; both are far longer than the line in circulation. Compare them side by side ↗

1957 — the compression appears, unsigned. Albert Szent-Györgyi uses “Research is to see what everybody has seen and think what nobody has thought” as a part epigraph in Bioenergetics — inside quotation marks, with no name attached. Wikiquote cites it to page 57 ↗

1958 — the credit slips, and “else” arrives. An untitled filler item in the Daily Standard of Sikeston, Missouri prints the epigraph as Szent-Györgyi’s own words and adds “else” — producing the exact wording quoted today. Quote Investigator dates it 29 December 1958 ↗
source.excerptNote: Schopenhauer’s German as reproduced by Quote Investigator ↗ from § 76 of the 1851 Hayn edition. Rendered literally: the task is not so much to see what no one has yet seen, as to think, about the thing everyone sees, what no one has yet thought — and that, he adds, is why it takes so much more to be a philosopher than a physicist. The second sentence is always dropped, and it is the one that changes the meaning.

source.rightsNote: Two different rights questions sit on this page, and only one has a clean answer. Schopenhauer’s 1851 German original is long out of copyright, and the excerpt above is quoted from that 1851 text. The famous English sentence is the uncertain part: no author or translator has ever been identified for it, its earliest documented appearance is as an unattributed epigraph in a 1957 book, and the traceable published translations of § 76 (Moll 1934, Bertalanffy 1952, Payne) are modern works with their own rights holders. We therefore assert no public-domain status for the popular wording.

author.name: Arthur Schopenhauer
author.kicker: The man whose thought it was
author.heading: About Arthur Schopenhauer
author.bio: Born in Danzig in 1788, Schopenhauer built his system in The World as Will and Representation (1818) and spent decades being ignored for it. Fame arrived only late, largely through Parerga und Paralipomena — the two-volume miscellany of essays and stray thoughts he published with A. W. Hayn of Berlin in 1851, nine years before his death. It is the book that made him quotable, and the book most of his circulating one-liners have been squeezed out of.

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit
misattribution.intro: This one drifted twice — once out of German into an English sentence nobody signed, and once off Schopenhauer onto a run of twentieth-century scientists.

items.why: The thought is his; the sentence is not. Schopenhauer wrote § 76 in German in 1851 and used no word for “research” anywhere in it. Quote Investigator ↗ prints three published English translations of the passage — Jan Willem Moll’s in 1934, Ludwig von Bertalanffy’s in 1952, and E. F. J. Payne’s — and every one of them is longer and clumsier than the line people quote.

The Hungarian Nobel laureate used the compressed sentence as an epigraph in Bioenergetics in 1957, but set it in quotation marks — the standard signal that he was quoting rather than coining. A Missouri newspaper dropped the quotation marks on 29 December 1958 ↗, added the word “else,” and the credit has stuck to him ever since.

A 2008 Biographical Encyclopedia of Scientists entry on Schrödinger carries a Bertalanffy-style rendering of the line. Quote Investigator ↗ treats the attribution as spurious, and the resemblance between “Schopenhauer” and “Schrödinger” is the obvious mechanism.

“Discovery consists of seeing what everybody has seen and thinking what nobody has thought” — a further rewrite trading “research” for “discovery” — is recorded in Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗ in a 1984 Foreign Affairs piece by Lewis Thomas. If you have seen this variant, it is a cousin of the same sentence, not a separate quotation.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is Schopenhauer’s, from 1851. The sentence people actually quote belongs to nobody in particular: its earliest documented appearance, on page 57 of Szent-Györgyi’s 1957 Bioenergetics ↗, is already inside quotation marks.

context.heading: A jab at physicists, not a research motto
lead: Schopenhauer’s § 76 is not advice for the laboratory. The sentence everybody quotes is only its first half; the half nobody quotes concludes that this is precisely why it takes so very much more to be a philosopher than a physicist. Cut that away, hand the remainder to a Nobel-winning biochemist, and you get something close to the opposite of what Schopenhauer meant — a compliment to science, extracted from a line written to needle it.

The compression is also what made it survive. The German is a coiling stack of subordinate clauses; the popular English form is fifteen words with a turn in the middle. Accurate translations of § 76 exist and have existed since at least 1934, and none of them ever caught on. The version that travelled is the one that reads like a slogan — which is exactly why it also travelled onto the wrong names.
context.detailsSummary: How one newspaper filler item created a Nobel laureate’s most famous quote
detailsBody: Szent-Györgyi did everything right. He used the line as an epigraph in Bioenergetics in 1957 and set it in quotation marks, the ordinary scholarly signal for these are not my words. What he did not do was name a source.

Per Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗, an untitled filler item in the Daily Standard of Sikeston, Missouri, on 29 December 1958 reprinted the epigraph as Szent-Györgyi’s own and slipped in the word “else.” That is the sentence in circulation today. By 1968 it was set in Evan Esar’s 20,000 Quips and Quotes under Szent-Györgyi’s name, and the quotation marks he had been careful to include were gone for good.
context.pull: The word ‘research’ appears nowhere in Schopenhauer’s sentence.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator traces this saying to Arthur Schopenhauer's Parerga und Paralipomena (1851), volume 2, section 76, page 93, published by A. W. Hayn in Berlin; gives the German verbatim including the following sentence about it taking more to be a philosopher than a physicist; documents translations by Jan Willem Moll (1934), Ludwig von Bertalanffy (1952) and E. F. J. Payne; records that Albert Szent-Gyorgyi printed the compressed form in Bioenergetics (1957) inside quotation marks; dates the 'everybody else' wording to an untitled filler item in the Daily Standard, Sikeston, Missouri, 29 December 1958; records Evan Esar's 20,000 Quips and Quotes (1968) crediting Szent-Gyorgyi; records a 1984 Lewis Thomas variant in Foreign Affairs; and treats the Erwin Schrodinger attribution (a 2008 Biographical Encyclopedia of Scientists entry) as spurious name confusion.

Wikiquote's Albert Szent-Gyorgyi page lists 'Research is to see what everybody has seen and think what nobody has thought' under its Quotes section, cited to Bioenergetics, Part II: Biological structures and functions, p. 57 (Academic Press, 1957).
Internet Archive holds a full scan of Albert Szent-Gyorgyi's Bioenergetics, published by Academic Press, New York, 1957.

Internet Archive holds a digitized copy of 'Parerga und Paralipomena: kleine philosophische Schriften' by Arthur Schopenhauer (1788-1860), published by A. W. Hayn, Berlin, 1851, with downloadable full text. (Note: the item carries no volume designation and its Fraktur OCR is unusable for text search, so it is offered as an edition artifact only, not as confirmation of the section 76 wording.)
Parerga and Paralipomena was published in 1851 in two volumes by Hayn of Berlin; volume 2 contains thirty-one topically organized sections; E. F. J. Payne produced an English translation.

Arthur Schopenhauer was a German philosopher and writer, born 22 February 1788 in Danzig and died 21 September 1860; his major work is The World as Will and Representation (1818) and he published the essay collection Parerga and Paralipomena in 1851.
Albert Szent-Gyorgyi (16 September 1893 - 22 October 1986) was a Hungarian biochemist who won the 1937 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, best known for first isolating vitamin C.

Wikiquote's Arthur Schopenhauer page collects his sourced quotations; a fetch of the page returned no entry matching the popular English 'Research is to see what everybody else has seen' wording, nor the 'task is not so much to see what no one has yet seen' formulation.
